title: Cello Concerto No. 1 in C major
hook: Written for a friend in Haydn’s orchestra, lost for two centuries, found in Prague in 1961.

painting.title: The Gore Family with George, third Earl Cowper
painting.collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
painting.pairingNote: A family making music around 1775, the father at the cello and his daughter at the keyboard; a decade earlier Haydn had written this concerto for the cellist of his prince’s orchestra.

facts: Haydn wrote the concerto in the early 1760s for Joseph Franz Weigl, a longtime friend and the principal cellist of Prince Nikolaus Esterházy’s orchestra, where Haydn worked. Around 1765 Haydn noted its opening theme in his own catalogue of his works.

Then the music disappeared. Only the theme in Haydn’s catalogue showed that it had existed, until 1961, when the musicologist Oldřich Pulkert found a copy in the National Museum in Prague. The first modern performance was given on 19 May 1962 by Miloš Sádlo with the Czechoslovak Radio Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Charles Mackerras. A few doubts have been raised about its authorship, but most experts accept it as Haydn’s.

The orchestra is small: strings, two oboes and two horns. The form still looks back to the Baroque concerto, with the orchestra’s refrain, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], framing the soloist’s passages.
It has since become a staple of the cello repertoire, recorded by Rostropovich, Jacqueline du Pré, Yo-Yo Ma and many others.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dignified, sunny march with brilliant solo writing (I), a long, quiet song for cello and strings (II), a breathless race (III).

movements.heading: Moderato
movements.summary: The orchestra opens with a firm, upright theme in dotted rhythms. When the cello enters it plays the same theme in rich chords on all four strings at once, and then shows off: rapid repeated notes, leaps between low and very high, long runs. One theme dominates the movement, broken into small pieces that Haydn develops one by one. Near the end the orchestra stops for the soloist’s [[cadenza|cadenza]].

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Rostropovich directs the Academy of St Martin in the Fields himself and plays cadenzas written by his friend Benjamin Britten, who had composed his Cello Symphony for him. His tempos are broad: the first movement lasts almost ten minutes. On the Spotify album the C major concerto is tracks 1–3, followed by the D major concerto.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: The oboes and horns fall silent; only the strings accompany the cello. After a calm opening for the strings, the cello enters on a single long note while the orchestra starts the theme again underneath it, and only then takes up the melody itself. Haydn repeats this gesture several times: the cello appears out of a held note, as if it had been listening. Near the end comes a second [[cadenza|cadenza]].

movements.heading: Allegro molto
movements.summary: A fast, bustling finale. The orchestra sets off alone, and once again the cello enters on a long note before racing away. It leaps so quickly between its low and high strings that it sounds like two instruments talking to each other. The last of the long-note entries is on a piercing high G.

mainIdeas.name: The running theme
mainIdeas.description: quick, driving notes in the violins, taken up by the cello.

mainIdeas.name: The two voices
mainIdeas.description: rapid jumps between the cello’s bass and treble, as if in conversation.

threads.title: The long note
threads.body: In all three movements the cello enters on a single sustained note. It is Haydn’s signature in this concerto.

threads.title: A friend’s instrument
threads.body: The concerto was written for a particular player, Weigl, and it is full of things he could do well: chords, fast repeated notes, very high passages.

threads.title: Lost and found
threads.body: For two centuries only a few notes in Haydn’s catalogue showed that this concerto had existed. Since 1962 it has become part of every cellist’s repertoire.
